chapter: Chicago clubs, entertainers and tent shows
title: Medicine shows with comedians, peppermint glass and snake oil
summary: Medicine wagons carried strong comedians and minstrel acts, with white talkers selling cures, and were not considered old fashioned.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Fights and things like that. And, we can go back to medicine shows, you know, did you ever hear for -- about the medicine shows?
I played a medicine show one, quite a few of them, yes.

Well, you see, there was the big wagon that'd pull up -- in the back of the wagon they let the tail down and set up curtains in the back, you know, draped the back with curtains and they'd have a comedian. Now these comedians most of them were very good comedians, and dancers, and joke tellers. And they sang a lot. Along the Johnny Hudgins type of a singer. Course, it wasn't pantomine, but they did -- had some of the best comedians, back in those days on medicine shows. It was a very good job.

And then, of course, the guys that were selling the medicine, naturally, he was white. A very good talker. Very good talker, he would sell his product. I remember one time they had a -- they were selling some kind of a glass that was made out of peppermint of some kind. This glass. And they would sell this glass, I guess maybe 50¢ or something 25¢ or 50¢, it was supposed to cure a lot of things and you poured water in it and then the water would, you know, take the taste of peppermint. From the glass. And it was supposed to be good for rheumatism and all that. And they sold a lot of that.
And so eventually you used up the

Oh, yes. Well, you know, after the show, you cut out cause the glass would probably disintegrate, or something, or warp or something. And they had snake oil, and all kind of -- for arthritis and rheumatism and they had bottles of bird medicines, for different type of ailments. Even tuberculosis they had things. And they did a big business. the talkers were very good confidence men. They would sell a lot of those bottles course the show would be first. Put the show on first. And some of them had tambourines and it was a minstrel type of entertainment. They would have on the back of these medicine wagons.
Now some of the people you performed with, when you were very young, must've been up in age then, they must've been people who really were from the former century, right?
They were up in age, that's right.
And what -- did their attitude, was there a generation gap, there? Were they considered old-fashioned, minstrel people?

No, they weren't considered old fashioned, not at that time, because that was the thing, minstrel shows and medicine wagons. That was the thing of the day. I wouldn't -- they weren't considered old fashioned at all. Cause people would look forward to these shows. Especially

medicine shows. Cause they had very good entertainment and I think some of our famous comedians doing their time on that medicine minstrel show -- that started out on medicine minstrel shows. Lot of them played washboards, and tambourines and they danced, told jokes, sang. I don't think they were considered -- no they weren't considered old fashioned because that was the thing during that time.
